post_title: Graduated from Rutgers with a Supply Chain degree. Seeing old threads about $70k entry level offers feels like gaslighting. Is the “top school” pipeline the only way left?
flattened_content:
Post Title: Graduated from Rutgers with a Supply Chain degree. Seeing old threads about $70k entry level offers feels like gaslighting. Is the “top school” pipeline the only way left?
Post Body: I need a reality check because I feel like I’m going crazy.

I graduated recently from Rutgers (Newark) with a Supply Chain degree. I know Rutgers is a solid school, but I’m starting to wonder if the location (Newark) is hurting me on paper compared to the main NB campus.

I’m currently looking at contract roles offering $24/hr with no benefits in this NJ/NY area. With the cost of living here, that is essentially poverty wages.

Meanwhile, I keep digging through old threads in this sub and others where people talk about walking into $65k-$75k entry level roles a few years ago like it was nothing. I also see posts in various supply chain communities where people claim they hit six figures in under two years at Fortune 500s.

I’m starting to get depressed because I feel like the only way to get those “large top company” roles paying $75k+ entry level is if you went to a specific top-tier feeder school. Am I right about this?

It feels like the golden ticket schools are:

· Penn State
· Michigan State
· University of Tennessee (Knoxville)
· MIT
· University of Arkansas
· Ohio State
· University of Michigan

Is the market just so saturated now that if you didn’t go to one of those specific "big name" programs, you’re stuck fighting over $24/hr contract gigs?

I don’t know what I’m doing wrong. I have the degree, I’m in a high-cost area willing to work, but I can’t even get a callback for the roles that used to be standard entry level.

How do I navigate this market? Is my degree useless if I didn’t go to a top 5 program?
Comment by Iiucwpost: No need to add Newark to your resume just state Rutgers University. The market is super tight for recent graduates. Keep applying and get some online certifications to boost your resume credentials. Hang in there - you got this
Comment by orgprof: This. And Rutgers Supply Chain has traditionally been among the top programs  in the country. Maybe do an online certificate in data analysis or AI if you have the time and dollars.
Comment by c961212: I second this. Rutgers Camden grad here, have just stated “Rutgers University” since I graduated 7 years ago and haven’t had any issues with it. Got into two ivies for grad school, and although the job market is tough, no employers have ever questioned my vague Rutgers campus affiliation lol
Comment by jcg878: It is not you or your school. The job market for new graduates is terrible and the economy is not as strong as advertised. Keep your chin up and hang in there.
Comment by jcg878: Also, keep in mind that you’re looking for your first job, not your last job. It gets easier eventually.
Comment by Throwrahj456: Are you sure about that? I’m already 27 almost 28. I graduated four years later than most people and I can’t even make good money which is what a lot of other people my age have a lot of other people are already at six figures at my age. I feel pathetic and like a loser.
Comment by Generic0323: You’re not a loser, don’t lose faith. Keep head down, keep applying and something will eventually go your way.

As others have mentioned the economy isn’t terribly strong right now, a lot of companies are taking a wait and see approach to hiring.
Comment by Old-School8916: comparison is the thief of all joy friend. take it from someone who graduated in 2009, right after the financial crisis, I compared myself to people who had graduated a few years before that. eventually opportunities will come your way if you *persist*.

here is one of my favorite quotes about this:  
*“Nothing in this world can take the place of persistence. Talent will not; nothing is more common than unsuccessful men with talent. Genius will not; unrewarded genius is almost a proverb. Education will not; the world is full of educated derelicts. Persistence and determination alone are omnipotent. The slogan 'Press On!' has solved and always will solve the problems of the human race.”*

*- President Calvin Coolidge*
Comment by orgprof: Yes.
Comment by Throwrahj456: Yeah, but right now I feel hopeless and suicidal not persistent like when is my life gonna finally get better if you actually knew my story not to be woe was me but can I finally have a life worth of living? Can I not be poor? Like that was the point of a fucking degree no offense not trying to curse at you. I’m just annoyed.
Comment by Old-School8916: well, the advice i gotta give is if you can, try to get into any role adjacent to supply chain at a larger company, even if the title isn't perfect. once you're inside a fortune 500, internal mobility is a whole different game. that's how most people actually eventually reach those salary numbers (outside of a few fields), not by walking in the front door at 22.

when i graduated the market was terrible, way worse than it is right now and I observed this first hand.

ur not a loser. you're job hunting in a down market with a useful degree. those are very different things.
Comment by orgprof: This is not bad advice. Even getting into a store management position at a place like Aldis for a year or two could put you into play for a career there. They are all about the supply chain.
Comment by Generic0323: Definitely not worth ending your life over — this is all temporary.

I graduated from RBS in 2014 with about $120k in student loans and started out in NYC making $55k. It took a while to feel comfortable, and honestly it felt like everyone around me had a head start — their school was paid for, they had nicer cars, and could go out all the time while I had to pass on a lot just to cover loans and rent.

It probably took me 7–8 years to really get to a good place. But once I paid off my student loans I could start saving money, and things picked up pretty quickly because of the habits and discipline I built along the way.

Not trying to make it about me — just want you to know you’re not alone. I’ve been through tough stretches too, and had similar thoughts at times. Just keep pushing — you’ll get there.
Comment by Ok_Supermarket5097: if you truly feel suicidal please reach out to a hotline or a therapist immediately
Comment by ApartmentWorried5692: Listen: I’m in college right now at 26 years old and I see tons of people my age making big bucks (I ignore those who struggle because I tend to only compare myself to who is ahead), and most of them are terrible with money. They blow it on dumb shit don’t save a lot. Very few people out there make a lot AND are money smart. The guys I know are blowing money for instagram shots only to not have a lot in the savings account after taxes, rent, necessities, etc.

If I were you, use your fully formed brain to your advantage and PLAN your life out before you make any big decisions like moving to the city or leasing a car. You know how many people graduate at 22 and think they know it all only to make a million mistakes only the real world and NOT Rutgers can teach? That’s exactly what they don’t show on instagram and it’s amusing seeing some of those flexxing people not post as much anymore. I wonder why…
Comment by Throwrahj456: OK on those people who make the big bucks how do they end up getting those top-tier jobs?
Comment by ApartmentWorried5692: Network, nepotism, linkedin, etc. You can also find subs on reddit for job searching. 

I’m at another school, but my professors seemed to be the ones who had the most connections with job offerings. I got on their good side and they even offered me internships last summer which i’m still kicking myself for not taking. Maybe reach out to a professor or two that you got along with.
Comment by yungfalafel: You are not a loser. I’m 28 right now and finishing my bachelors after a number of years working dead end retail jobs and going to community college. Everybody takes their own time. I used to think the same as you, but I realised that hating myself for not “succeeding” did nothing except make me more angry and bitter. 

It might be frustrating to take one step at a time when it feels like you’ve been waiting at the starting line forever, but there’s no other way to move forward. Plus, you are entering a historically bad job market. Don’t be too hard on yourself
Comment by SteveMcgooch: I graduated from Rutgers Newark in 2019 at the age 25. I didn't find full time work until the spring of 2021 and have now been with my company for 5 years. It takes time, global economics and politics will affect every step of the way. Keep your chin up
Comment by Throwrahj456: What was your major was it supply chain like me? Also, what was your GPA? And did anyone ever ask what campus you graduated from? Was there a stigma that you went to Newark over NB? Also, when you finally found a role was it good pay or a lowball cause bro like I’m not having any luck as you see from my post :(
Comment by SteveMcgooch: Management Information Systems. 3.87 GPA, I flunked out of WVU after 3 years. Attended county for 2 and Rutgers for 2. Graduated Summa Cum Laude. No one ever asked which campus I attended when it mattered in interviews. I took work at a temp agency after COVID and landed a full time gig with shit pay but for a good company. After 2 years I doubled my pay at that company and entered not total shit pay area. Everyone's pay is different, just like everyone's story is different. Show up put in the work, put in the hours, and everything will work itself out. Yes it will be stressful

Comment by Siakim43: Imagine how Comp Sci students feel. Being told their whole lives to "learn to code" and everything will be OK. Even President Biden was pushing this "learn to code" message.


Now those kids, who've been told their whole lives to "learn to code and everything will be alright" find themselves with no job opportunities despite being some of the brightest kids in the classroom. It's such a bad situation - I can't even imagine how bitter I'd feel if I was a part of this cohort of kids/young adults...
Comment by jd732: And before that there was Clinton “just go to college and everything will be alright” as EPA regulations sent manufacturing to Mexico.

Comment by Throwrahj456: And if they ask, what do I say?
Comment by Mxrlinox: Unlikely scenario but that’s when you’d share your campus. Only share if asked
Comment by YourWifesBull666: They won’t.
Comment by goosedog79: Over 20 years ago, I graduated from Livingston college- they were trying to rebrand it as the “non black school” and we were always told just say you went to RU anyway.
Comment by jd732: I’ve been lying about my GPA for 32 years. Nobody ever called my bluff on 3.85.
Comment by theshortgrace: I just realized i can do this lol 😂
Comment by Siakim43: Tough market, it's so hard to break in for new grads. Rutgers Supply Chain is also top tier and my friend has been making six figures for awhile now with that degree.
Comment by Throwrahj456: Yeah, that’s why I majored in it on this even though I went to Newark cause New Brunswick sucks. with transferred credit what do I do to get on that pathway in three years or less like all your friends to start at 75K and then see 110 K year three and then maybe 150 K year five?
Comment by Siakim43: A lot has to do with timing that's out of your control. Know that it's not your fault - you didn't choose when to be born.

Comment by Throwrahj456: I’m 27 years old I should’ve graduated three years ago, but I only graduated now because New Brunswick screwed me over with transfer credits and I didn’t know about Newark. I didn’t know that it was one business school, but both campuses were very different with their credit transfer restrictions that’s why I graduated at 26 instead of 23 when the job market was better and now my entire life is fucked and I feel hopeless every day.
Comment by shredfasteatass: Let me assure you you're not alone. I started my undergraduate in rutgers NB after transferring in at 22. Graduated at 26. Took part time roles in corporate making $22 an hour and gained experience and grinded working my way up. 3 years of that and finally touched 65k. Got laid off from the pandemic and came back to a 50k role after 9 months unemployed. Worked my way up for another 3 years to 80k and then got laid off from a re org do to budget cuts. 60% of my company gone. Unemployed after that for 7 months and took a new role for 55k. Just this year finally found the dream job all my years of experience set me up for and now jumped up to 150k. The path will not be straight forward but you need to take those shit roles and gain whatever you can for now and find a way.
Comment by Throwrahj456: What industry do you work in supply chain? Also, can I see your résumé or can I DM you?
Comment by YourW1feandK1ds: If it helps I graduated late with a degree in Philosophy (oddly useful) and a degree in ITI (incredible bullshit). I started working in as Tier 2 help desk analyst and then leveraged that into a Trade Ops role at a trading firm and then leveraged that into a SWE role at the same trading firm. 

Just start anywhere doing something tangentially related. You can use the experience to leverage into a role closer to what you want to do (assuming good performance). The important thing is to start
Comment by Throwrahj456: Thanks for sharing, so what do I do?
Comment by YourW1feandK1ds: Take the jobs that pay less. The question you ask yourself should be "can i leverage this job for a better job in the future". Not "is this the job that I want".
Comment by Beneficial-Fish-4722: yep this. if the jobs you want arent possible rn, take adjacent jobs if possible and leverage those into the jobs you want later on
Comment by Its_kinda_nice_out: Dude you just posted the same question like 3 days ago, now you’re posting your resume on the internet.  Three final pieces of advice for you since you didn’t listen to my advice last time.


1.  Relax.  Please go touch grass.  You’re making this way harder on yourself than it needs to be and i bet it’s impacting your ability to sell yourself as a candidate.

2.  Learn to make decisions for yourself.  This entire thread is you asking people “what do i do now?”  Youre an adult.  Figure it out!  Employers dont want people that need to be guided every step of the way.

3.  Redo your entire resume.  First, the format is probably getting you screened out of all AI bots because it’s unreadable.  Second, your content lacks content.  You’re matter of factly explaining what you did, not why or what your successes were.  Google what a good resume looks like and how to write one.  If you need to, pay somebody to fix it.


I’m sorry you’re going through a tough time, but nobody can help you but yourself.  Good luck.

Now people would dream of that. It's a different reality and people that graduated before shit hit the fan are so lucky
Comment by PapaRayneski: Hang in there. Saw you said you feel pathetic, don't. Be proactive, it's all you can do. Be a "loser" on linkedin, connect with Rutgers alum and ask for referrals. I want you to know there are literally two perspectives for fresh grads right now, you are either cracked and get a top tier job, or you are struggling for months to find a job. The pipelines for pretty much every career path are getting squeezed dramatically. People will say ai, out sourcing or whatever but the reality is people who graduated a mere 4 years ago were applying to a market where employers were eager to train people up and let them grow into roles. Not recruiters are looking for people who can do the job tmrw. It sucks, but we need to play the hand we are dealt. The game has been rigged from the start, so we must learn how to play it.
Comment by undergroundmusic69: Hey OP, just sharing some wisdom. I graduated engineering in the early 2010’s when the job market was still recovering from 2008. It took me 2 years to get my first big boy job. It absolutely sucked and was demoralizing. 

What helped me out a lot, was staying close to my friends and network. When I finally got a job, it was through a fraternity brother who had gotten promoted and his old job was opening up. I am still with that company to this day. Don’t be afraid to take on low paying jobs to keep the lights on. I worked as a cashier for a while in a pharmacy and it gave me skills to talk about in my interview. 

You will grow and you will succeed, but life is not the linear path schools talk to you about. Chin up friend — you got this!

What they did, their history, their competition. Have an intelligent question or two to ask when it came time to ask.  Look motivated. One guy actually said 'WoW'.  and then I got a 'WoW' offer.

It’s one business school, but RBS is very different with both campuses now finally the policies changed last summer but in 2020 when I was 21 New Brunswick was really strict with transferred credits and I went to TCNJ for a semester in 2021 dropped out then worked in tech sales lost my job my uncle got leukemia and I had a nervous breakdown and before that I also was homeless, and I had other severe mental health, trauma and family trauma, which is why I have a lot of gaps. Comment by Illustrious-Chip-245: As a hiring manager I could give two fucks about policies and campuses. I’m not trying to be harsh, but you need to do a better job of telling your story. If you haven’t had a job in that time, you should take whatever comes your way just to build a work history.

Maybe in North Jersey/ NYC you’ll find 65k-75k but that’s if you have connections and experience.  Just start from low and you work your way up.  That’s the reality.
Comment by Throwrahj456: Yeah, I’m open to that but that’s 10 or $20,000 less like I got a contract role that’s $46,000. I can’t live off that in a New Jersey 65K is decent.
Comment by NoDay3849: It’s okay.  I’m so also in supply chain.
I started with 45k and worked my way up.  
It’s all a process.  Best of luck.
Comment by SeBass94: Applied to 100+ jobs when I graduated with a liberal arts degree, got interviews for like 3, hired at 1. Got my foot in the door and now I’m in finance. Hang in there, don’t be afraid to take a non-perfect role for a few months and keep looking. It’s tough out there.
Comment by Kitler0327: I graduated from Rutgers NB with a supply chain degree back in spring of 2022. It took me six months to land a job and even then it was only $52k. I was there for 2.5 years and two promotions and when I left I was making $70k.

The job I left for was $90k. I was only there about six months. I had been looking for a new gig since August and just finally accepted a new role at $80k. The market is really hard right now,  it's not just you.
Comment by AstutelyInane: >Is the market just so saturated now that ~~if you didn’t go to one of those specific "big name" programs,~~ you’re stuck fighting over $24/hr contract gigs?

This happened with CS a few years back too. I remember seeing many posts where it seemed like ***everyone*** was coming out and making 6 figures at their first job. The reality was never that rosy for most people, but the top people post proudly and others...don't as much. 

HS students read all those posts and figured CS was the golden ticket. When there has been a hiring boon for a couple of years, the market just can't handle the graduating classes of 500 in that one major from every large school, so the top jobs still only go to the top 2-3 graduates from each school and the rest take what they can get, sometime in other fields for hourly wages.

I would also mention that what goes on in politics matters too.  It matters whether there is a general feeling of societal stability or turmoil. It's a tough time to be on the job market right now because companies tend to pare their workforce during economic uncertainty (wars, changing regulations, volatile markets, etc.)
Comment by PotentialAccident339: Graduated from Newark in '16. Got a job through career services (they had on-campus events at Newark). $68k starting salary plus $5k signing bonus at a big 4 financial firm.
Comment by Deku-Butler: Imma be honest, it took me 10 years to make $70k a year with an undergraduate business degree. Unfortunately, internship and resume prestige matter a lot for business grads. I worked retail and went to a D3 state school, so my first couple jobs out of school weren’t exactly that helpful besides helping me get to where I am now.
Comment by Middle-Attention6711: Here is something I learned years ago about job hunting. Make a list of companies that are in your field. Go to each website and click on employment opportunities. Search for openings and apply right through their website.
I found success this way rather than indeed, for example. Best of luck, you got this!!
Comment by BoxBasic4408: You have to thread the needle of finding the right company. You will be swamped with $25hr offers, and why not if they can get you that cheap then why not(if you have to take it then do so but keep aggressively looking all the while).
My recommendation is to research European based companies and focus applying to these as they will be more receptive to your supply chain understanding rather than your school choice.
Comment by redditnewbie_: Dude ur not ahead nor behind. You’re exactly where you need to be. Sucks, yes, but welcome to the club. If you cannot keep your head right during times of struggle, life will only get harder. Luckily, your 20s are the exact time you learn. If successful, you will have a stress management system rigid enough to carry you through the uncertainties you will invariably encounter. For the rest of your life.
